support.p: National Monuments Service SMR ID: CO085-067007-

supportDesc.condition: Reused as a lintel in a souterrain, the stone is rough and irregular, and it is difficult to discriminate between letters and natural markings on its surface (Macalister 1945, 100).

layoutDesc.layout: There appear to be two inscriptions on this stone. The longer inscription (1) is inscribed on the dexter angle of the main face, running over the top diagonally, and down the dexter angle of the parallel face of the stone (Macalister 1945, 98). The second, shorter inscriptions (2) runs upwards on the angle in between. Macalister (1945, 100) also describes what he calls ogham graffito in the middle of the B-surface (i.e. to the right of the shorter inscription (2).

handDesc.handNote: The inscription is coarsely pocked in bold, well-spaced strokes. Macalister's graffito is impossible to decipher (or even to be sure of) considering the roughness of the stone.

origin.origPlace: Ballyhank (Baile Sheanc), Co. Cork, Ireland 51.831516, -8.609832 ITM Coordinates: 557971, 564534
origin.origDate: Possibly mid to early second half of the sixth century

history.provenance: Discovered in 1846 by Cork antiquarians Windele, Abell, and Hawkes in a souterrain (CO085-067002-) in the SW quadrant of a ringfort (CO085-067001-), with five other ogham stones: I-COR-046, I-COR-047, I-COR-048, I-COR-049 and I-COR-051. In 1849 Windele removed five of the stones, including this one, to his own residence (Blair's Castle, Cork) but they were later moved to the museum of the Royal Irish Academy (Brash 1879, 140; Macalister 1945, 92-93).

All six stones from Ballyhank are now in the collection of the National Museum of Ireland. This stone was recorded in 3D in 2015 as part of the Ogham in 3D project in collaboration with the Discovery Programme.

app.note: In the main inscription (1), Macalister (1945, 99) suggests that DOMANEQI may be an error for DOMANENI. Considering its location on the stone, as the inscription turns downwards from the top, the carver may have confused the orientation of the scores, as seen in other examples (e.g. I-KER-012 Arraglen, Co. Kerry).

div.p: The binomial name MAQI-ESEA is not continued in Old Irish and so the name Mac-Eisse is unattested (indicated by the *). None of Ziegler’s (1994, 180) tentative suggestions for its interpretation, i.e., containing es ‘waterfall’ or es ‘stoat, weasel’, are convincing. However, alternative explanations of ESEA are formally possible. It could be the genitive of Old Irish és ‘track, trace’, or it could be the genitive of éissi ‘reins’.

If taken at face value, the Q of DOMANEQI can be a hypercorrect spelling for the common Old Irish adjectival suffix -ch, that would normally be written with C (ᚉ) in ogham. The name would thus be an adjectival derivative in -ach of domun < *dubno- ‘deep, world’ (which has some probelms), or an early representative of Old Irish domnach ‘Sunday; church’, ultimately from Latin dominicus. The analysis as a formation from *dubno- entails the assumption of an anaptyctic or intrusive vowel (Eska 2012, 3 ). This analysis, however, leaves a number of issues unaddressed. If the identification of the suffix is correct, the spelling with E is unusual, unless it is a lowered *i, perhaps shortened from *ī, and thus presupposing an original suffix *-iko- or *-īko-, not *-āko-. Also, Domnach (< Lat. dominicus) does not seem to be attested as a personal name in Old Irish. Ziegler (1994, 168) cites it as the name of a Pictish king in the Irish translation of Nennius’ Historia Britonum (Gartnait f. Domnach; eDIL dil.ie/18125), but this is an error for Gartnait mac Domnaill. The saints’ name Mo Domnóc is outwardly similar (Fél. 13 Feb., 18 May), but differs in having the British loan suffix -óc instead of the native Irish -ach. Macalister (1945, 99) offers no analysis for his alternative reading of the name as DOMANENI. It could be compared with the population name Fir Domnann and the British Dumnonii (> *dubnon-(i̭)o-, even though the suffixal vowels do not match). This analysis likewise entails the assumption of A being an anaptyctic vowel.

For the obscure element MAD in the second inscription, the only approximate parallel in Old Irish is the kin-group name Uí Maidnáin (CGH 481), maybe related to the root *mad- ‘to break’ (cf. OIr. maidid ‘to break’).

The analysis of DOMANEQI as a name with the suffix *-ko- would date the inscription after the merger of *ku̯ and *k in the early 6th century. If the name continues *dubno- ‘world’, it presupposes lowering of *u > *o, and perhaps also shortening of *ī > *i and the subsequent lowering to *e. ESEA also seems to display lowering of *i > *e in the suffix, whatever its etymology is. This speaks more for the mid-6th century or its early second half. In this case, the retained -I of DOMANEQI must be viewed as a conscious archaisation.
